Title: Significance of Brettanomyces and Dekkera during winemaking: a synoptic review.
Snippet: Brettanomyces/Dekkera spp. have long been known for their ability to affect wine quality negatively through the formation of acetic acid, which constitutes more than 90% of wine's volatile acidity (VA) (Van der Walt & Van Kerken, 1958). Elevated levels of acetic acid can be detrimental to wine quality as it imparts a vinegary/ acetone-like aroma (Eglinton & Henschke, 1999) and has also been associated with sluggish/stuck fermentations (Bisson, 1999). Brettanomyces/Dekkera yeasts have a particular metabolism that enables them to produce acetic acid (Licker et al. 1998;Loureiro & Malfeito-Ferreira, 2006). M.T.J. Custers was the first to describe that the presence of oxygen stimulated glucose fermentation and that this led to the introduction of a biochemical characteristic known as the "negative Pasteur effect" (or 'Custers' effect') (Scheffers & Wiken, 1969;Wijsman et al., 1984;Licker et al., 1998). Custers also determined that several strains of Brettanomyces were capable of producing considerable quantities of acetic acid under conditions of aerobiosis and found that anaerobic conditions inhibited glucose fermentation (Licker et al. 1998). 

Recently, studies have shown that the availability of oxygen presents a favourable scenario for the development of Brettanomyces/Dekkera yeasts during winemaking as it supports their growth and survival and also acetic acid production (Ciani et al., 1997;Freer et al., 2003;Aguilar-Uscanga et al., 2003). In contrast, anaerobosis during alcoholic fermentation may well impede Brettanomyces/Dekkera growth, but would not necessarily prevent their development (Ciani et al., 1997). Therefore, the risk involved with VA formation by Brettanomyces/Dekkera spp. can be reduced by minimising the wine's exposure to oxygen (during racking and transfers) in combination with effective SO 2 usage (Du Toit et al. 2005).

Title: Combine Use of Selected Schizosaccharomyces pombe and Lachancea thermotolerans Yeast Strains as an Alternative to the Traditional Malolactic Fermentation in Red Wine Production
Snippet: Most red wines commercialized in the market use the malolactic fermentation process in order to ensure stability from a microbiological point of view. In this second fermentation, malic acid is converted into l-lactic acid under controlled setups. However this process is not free from possible collateral effects that on some occasions produce off-flavors, wine quality loss and human health problems. In warm viticulture regions such as the south of Spain, the risk of suffering a deviation during the malolactic fermentation process increases due to the high must pH. This contributes to produce wines with high volatile acidity and biogenic amine values. This manuscript develops a new red winemaking methodology that consists of combining the use of two non-Saccharomyces yeast strains as an alternative to the traditional malolactic fermentation. In this method, malic acid is totally consumed by Schizosaccharomyces pombe, thus achieving the microbiological stabilization objective, while Lachancea thermotolerans produces lactic acid in order not to reduce and even increase the acidity of wines produced from low acidity musts. This technique reduces the risks inherent to the malolactic fermentation process when performed in warm regions. The result is more fruity wines that contain less acetic acid and biogenic amines than the traditional controls that have undergone the classical malolactic fermentation.

Summary
Non-Saccharomyces yeasts influence wine acidity through two major pathways: volatile acidity (primarily acetic and related oxygen-dependent metabolism) and titratable acidity (malic/citric acid degradation and conversion to lactic/other acids), with outcomes that are strongly strain-, stage-, and oxygen-dependent. When competing mechanisms align—for example, oxygen exposure that stimulates acetic acid production versus anaerobic fermentation that suppresses growth, or biological MLF-like conversions that reduce malic acid while co-inoculation lowers acetic acid—mechanistic “neutralization” can yield wines with acceptable acidity and sensory profile. <cite id="5ef2f7f7-0">Historically, non-Saccharomyces yeasts were linked to elevated acetic acid and volatile acidity, but effects depend on strain and fermentative strategy, with co-inoculation and sequential fermentations able to keep volatile acidity below thresholds and selected strains providing balanced profiles</cite>. <cite id="5ef2f7f7-2">Industrial use of non-Saccharomyces is now common to modulate acidity, with species like Torulaspora delbrueckii, Lachancea thermotolerans, Metschnikowia, and Pichia used to decrease titratable acidity via malic/citric acid degradation while improving mouthfeel and reducing ethanol</cite>.

Mechanisms that increase volatile acidity (acetic acid) and the role of oxygen
Brettanomyces/Dekkera yeasts are canonical producers of volatile acidity, with acetic acid often exceeding 90% of total volatile acidity in affected wines. Their metabolism generates acetic acid, and they exhibit a “negative Pasteur effect”: oxygen stimulates glucose fermentation and acetic acid production, whereas anaerobiosis inhibits fermentation and reduces acetic acid formation. Winemaking oxygen exposure therefore increases risk, while anaerobic conditions during alcoholic fermentation impede growth though not always entirely prevent development. Risk mitigation combines minimizing oxygen exposure and effective SO2 management. <cite id="a6a66f7b-0">Brettanomyces/Dekkera affect wine quality via acetic acid that can exceed 90% of volatile acidity; oxygen stimulates glucose fermentation and acetic acid production (Custers effect), whereas anaerobiosis inhibits fermentation; minimizing oxygen exposure and using SO2 reduces VA risk</cite>. <cite id="a6a66f7b-2">Oxygen promotes Brettanomyces growth and acetic acid production in must and wine, while SO2 rapidly kills these yeasts; micro-oxygenation can increase Brettanomyces counts unless SO2 is maintained</cite>. <cite id="a6a66f7b-4">Micro-oxygenation increased Brettanomyces from 10^1 to 10^3 cfu/mL over 14 weeks, with concurrent decreases in free SO2; re-adjusting SO2 curtailed growth, illustrating oxygen’s supportive role alongside SO2 control</cite>.

Other non-Saccharomyces genera can contribute to volatile acidity, but profiles vary by strain and matrix. Selected Lachancea/Schizosaccharomyces combinations can stabilize acidity without increasing acetic acid, highlighting that not all non-Saccharomyces elevate VA. <cite id="10a142bb-0">Combinations of non-Saccharomyces yeasts produced higher glycerol and pyruvic acid without increasing acetic acidity and with reduced ethanol; Schizosaccharomyces pombe plus Lachancea thermotolerans stabilized wines from a malic acid standpoint without MLF</cite>. <cite id="5ef2f7f7-0">Certain strains like Hanseniaspora pseudoguilliermondii can show high acetic acid, but Candida zemplinina reached the highest reported volatile acidity (1.37 g/L) without sensory defect; co-inoculation with Saccharomyces reduced final acetic acid by 10–18%; sequential fermentations with Kazachstania, Torulaspora, and Aureobasidium maintained VA below thresholds while boosting glycerol and lowering final alcohol</cite>.

Mechanisms that decrease titratable acidity and adjust pH
Non-Saccharomyces yeasts can lower titratable acidity by metabolizing malic and citric acids, reducing the buffering capacity of organic acids and thereby lowering measured acidity. Mixed-culture and sequential fermentations with Torulaspora delbrueckii, Lachancea thermotolerans, Metschnikowia pulcherrima, Pichia kluyveri, and others decrease titratable acidity, often concurrently reducing ethanol and increasing glycerol, which improves mouthfeel. <cite id="5ef2f7f7-3">Titratable acidity decreased in blueberry wine with T. delbrueckii compared to Saccharomyces, attributed to decreased malic and citric acids; Pichia fermentans strongly degraded citric acid; H. uvarum and M. pulcherrima reduced titratable acidity in peach wine, mainly via malic acid reduction</cite>. <cite id="5ef2f7f7-2">Deacidification by yeasts degrades L-malic acid, reduces titratable acidity, and lowers ethyl carbamate risk; industrial strains (T. delbrueckii, L. thermotolerans, M. pulcherrima, P. kluyveri) modify acidity and mouthfeel while decreasing ethanol</cite>.

Some non-Saccharomyces perform “biological MLF” or mimic it: Schizosaccharomyces pombe consumes malic acid, while Lachancea thermotolerans produces lactic acid, increasing acidity in low-acid musts and stabilizing wine without added bacteria. Ethanol from alcoholic fermentation and glycerol from yeast metabolism can also shift pH and perceived acidity; careful strain selection and co-fermentation can reduce final alcohol while maintaining acidity balance. <cite id="10a142bb-0">S. pombe plus L. thermotolerans reduced malic acid without MLF, stabilized wines, and lowered biogenic amines, with higher glycerol and reduced ethanol; L. thermotolerans had lower SO2 demand</cite>. <cite id="10a142bb-1">Benito et al. describe an S. pombe–L. thermotolerans strategy: malic acid is consumed by S. pombe while L. thermotolerans generates lactic acid to increase acidity in low-acid musts as an MLF alternative</cite>. <cite id="5ef2f7f7-0">Lachancea thermotolerans is noted for high lactic acid production in biological acidification, enabling acidity increases in low-acid matrices</cite>.

Beyond direct acid conversion, fermentation processes alter acidity measurements and perception. CO2 evolution from malolactic fermentation (or biological lactic acid production) reduces titratable acidity by converting malic to lactic, while ethanol and glycerol act as weak buffers influencing pH and astringency. Temperature, oxygen, and nutrient conditions modulate enological outcomes. <cite id="10a142bb-0">Non-Saccharomyces co-fermentations produced higher glycerol and pyruvic acid without increasing acetic acid, with reduced ethanol; L. thermotolerans produced lower SO2 demand</cite>. <cite id="5ef2f7f7-3">Lower malic and citric acids after non-Saccharomyces fermentation correlate with decreased titratable acidity and improved mouthfeel in berry wines</cite>. <cite id="a6a66f7b-0">Acetic acid is the principal volatile acidity component in VA-dominant wines, with oxygen exposure favoring acetic acid formation</cite>.

Competing mechanisms and when they “neutralize” each other
Oxygen vs. anaerobiosis: Oxygen exposure favors Brettanomyces growth and acetic acid production (negative Pasteur effect), whereas anaerobic alcoholic fermentation conditions inhibit their fermentation, limiting acetic acid formation and VA rise. If oxygen ingress is minimized (short transfers, micro-oxygenation controlled) and SO2 is sufficient, the risk of oxygen-driven acetic acidification is curtailed; conversely, if oxygen persists and SO2 is low, Brettanomyces proliferation and acetic acid accumulation dominate. <cite id="a6a66f7b-0">Oxygen stimulates glucose fermentation and acetic acid production in Brettanomyces; anaerobiosis inhibits fermentation; minimizing oxygen and using SO2 reduces VA risk</cite>. <cite id="a6a66f7b-2">Oxygen increases Brettanomyces growth and acetic acid production; SO2 rapidly kills these yeasts; micro-oxygenation raises counts unless SO2 is maintained</cite>. <cite id="a6a66f7b-4">Measured increases in Brettanomyces under controlled oxygen dosing and concurrent SO2 drops, then suppression after SO2 correction, illustrate the balance between oxygen-driven proliferation and SO2 control</cite>.

Biological conversion vs. spoilage risk: Malolactic fermentation converts malic to lactic acid, lowering titratable acidity; however, acetic acid bacteria and Brettanomyces can elevate VA if oxygen and nutrition are conducive. Using non-Saccharomyces to achieve MLF-like outcomes (S. pombe consuming malic acid; L. thermotolerans producing lactic acid) can “neutralize” the need for MLF while avoiding off-flavors and biogenic amine increases, especially in warm, high-pH regions. <cite id="10a142bb-0">S. pombe plus L. thermotolerans stabilized wines without MLF, with reduced ethanol and biogenic amines, and acidity increased in low-acid musts via lactic acid production</cite>. <cite id="10a142bb-1">An alternative to MLF used malic acid consumption by S. pombe and lactic acid production by L. thermotolerans to raise acidity in low-acid musts</cite>. <cite id="a6a66f7b-3">In warm regions, traditional MLF risks off-flavors and higher volatile acidity/biogenic amines; the combined non-Saccharomyces approach reduced acetic acid and biogenic amines compared to MLF controls</cite>.

Strain selection and co-inoculation vs. acid accumulation: Selected non-Saccharomyces strains and co-inoculation with Saccharomyces can suppress acetic acid accumulation while enabling deacidification, effectively neutralizing competing tendencies for VA rise and titratable acidity decrease. <cite id="5ef2f7f7-0">Co-inoculation of strain QTX-C10 with Saccharomyces reduced acetic acid by 10.81–17.78%; sequential inoculation with Kazachstania, Torulaspora, and Aureobasidium kept VA below thresholds while increasing glycerol and lowering final alcohol</cite>. <cite id="5ef2f7f7-2">Selected non-Saccharomyces can control acidity and mouthfeel while decreasing ethanol, offering deacidification benefits without spoilage risks when strains are well-chosen</cite>. <cite id="10a142bb-0">All non-Saccharomyces fermentations in a Tempranillo case produced higher glycerol/pyruvic acid without increasing acetic acidity and with reduced ethanol, indicating successful mitigation of acid-boosting pathways</cite>.

Succinic acid contribution: Some non-Saccharomyces (e.g., Torulaspora delbrueckii, Candida stellata) produce succinic acid, which contributes to total acidity but has a salty/bitter-acid sensory character that can become negative at high levels. This represents a competing mechanism: titratable acidity increases, but sensory balance may deteriorate if overproduced. <cite id="a6a66f7b-1">T. delbrueckii and C. stellata can form succinic acid, contributing to total acidity with a salty/bitter-acid taste that can negatively influence quality at excessive levels</cite>.

Practical timing and management: 
- During alcoholic fermentation: Anaerobic conditions suppress Brettanomyces activity, aiding control of volatile acidity; co-fermentations with malolactic-like non-Saccharomyces (S. pombe, L. thermotolerans) can reduce malic acid and produce lactic acid, lowering titratable acidity and stabilizing pH/mouthfeel. <cite id="a6a66f7b-0">Anaerobiosis during alcoholic fermentation impedes Brettanomyces growth and acetic acid formation</cite>. <cite id="10a142bb-0">Co-fermentation with S. pombe and L. thermotolerans reduced malic acid and ethanol, stabilized acidity without MLF, and lowered SO2 demand</cite>.
- Post-fermentation/storage: Oxygen ingress favors acetic acid bacteria and Brettanomyces, elevating VA unless SO2 and closure practices limit exposure; maintaining sufficient free SO2 and limiting oxygen permeation prevents neutralization of control by oxygen-driven spoilage. <cite id="a6a66f7b-2">Oxygen supports Brettanomyces growth and acetic acid production; SO2 rapidly kills cells; oxygen permeation via oak supports survival</cite>. <cite id="a6a66f7b-4">Micro-oxygenation increased Brettanomyces counts when SO2 was low; maintaining SO2 restored control</cite>.
- Low-acid musts: Introducing Lactobacillus/Lachancea-like acidification via biological MLF can increase acidity and improve structure without added bacteria, counteracting the tendency toward flatness under climate change. <cite id="5ef2f7f7-1">Non-Saccharomyces are used to modulate acidity to meet consumer preferences for lower ethanol and better mouthfeel, especially as climate change yields flatter-acid wines</cite>. <cite id="10a142bb-1">L. thermotolerans produces lactic acid to raise acidity in low-acid musts as an MLF alternative</cite>.

Key examples of “neutralization” points
- Winemaking window: If oxygen exposure is minimized during and immediately after alcoholic fermentation while SO2 is adequate, the oxygen-driven acetic acid production by Brettanomyces is curtailed, and co-inoculation/deacidification by non-Saccharomyces can reduce malic acid; together, these competing mechanisms can yield wines with stable titratable acidity and low VA. <cite id="a6a66f7b-0">Reducing oxygen and using SO2 limits VA formation by Brettanomyces</cite>. <cite id="5ef2f7f7-0">Co-inoculation and sequential strategies reduced acetic acid and kept VA below thresholds</cite>.
- Warm, high-pH vintages: Choosing S. pombe for malic acid consumption paired with L. thermotolerans for lactic acid production can “neutralize” the risk of MLF deviations and low-acid profile, reducing acetic acid and biogenic amines compared to traditional MLF. <cite id="a6a66f7b-3">In warm regions, traditional MLF can raise VA and biogenic amines; the combined non-Saccharomyces approach produced wines with less acetic acid and less risk</cite>. <cite id="10a142bb-0">The combined strategy stabilized acidity without MLF and reduced ethanol and biogenic amines</cite>.
- Sensory balance: Even when titratable acidity is reduced via malic acid metabolism, overproduction of succinic or higher alcohols can unbalance acidity perception; selecting strains with low SO2 demand and moderate higher-alcohol profiles helps prevent this. <cite id="a6a66f7b-1">Some non-Saccharomyces increase higher alcohols; careful strain choice is needed to avoid sensory imbalance</cite>. <cite id="a6a66f7b-1">T. delbrueckii and C. stellata produce succinic acid that aids acidity but can be undesirable at high levels</cite>.

Caveats and uncertainties
Outcomes are highly strain- and matrix-dependent: the same genus can either raise or moderate acidity depending on clone, inoculum, and co-fermentation strategy. Reported reductions in acetic acid via co-inoculation and sequential fermentations are promising but require matching winery hygiene and oxygen control to avoid Brettanomyces resurgence. Additionally, while biological acidification can raise lactic acid, sensory impacts (e.g., salty/bitter notes from succinate or medicinal/vinous phenols) demand careful monitoring and strain selection. <cite id="5ef2f7f7-0">Non-Saccharomyces effects on acetic acid vary by strain and strategy; co-inoculation reduced acetic acid by 10–18%, and selected sequential fermentations kept VA below thresholds</cite>. <cite id="a6a66f7b-1">Brettanomyces can contribute desirable or undesirable characters; low-level “Brett” may add complexity in some reds</cite>. <cite id="a6a66f7b-2">Oxygen and SO2 management is critical; micro-oxygenation and SO2 dynamics directly influence VA risk</cite>.

Practical takeaways
- To lower volatile acidity: minimize oxygen exposure and maintain adequate free SO2, especially during transfers and maturation; employ anaerobic conditions where feasible; select non-Saccharomyces with low acetic acid profiles and high glycerol production. <cite id="a6a66f7b-0">Minimizing oxygen and using SO2 reduces VA risk by Brettanomyces</cite>. <cite id="5ef2f7f7-0">Selected strains and co-inoculation reduced acetic acid and maintained sensory quality</cite>.
- To reduce titratable acidity and improve mouthfeel: use mixed or sequential fermentations with T. delbrueckii, L. thermotolerans, M. pulcherrima, Pichia kluyveri; consider S. pombe–L. thermotolerans pairings to mimic MLF and raise acidity in low-acid lots. <cite id="5ef2f7f7-2">Yeast deacidification reduces malic acid, titratable acidity, and ethyl carbamate risk, improving mouthfeel</cite>. <cite id="10a142bb-1">S. pombe consumes malic acid; L. thermotolerans produces lactic acid to increase acidity in low-acid musts</cite>. <cite id="5ef2f7f7-3">Non-Saccharomyces decreased titratable acidity by degrading malic and citric acids across fruit wines</cite>.
- Competing mechanisms “neutralize” each other when oxygen-driven acetic acid production is constrained (by anaerobiosis and SO2) while acid-consumption/conversion pathways are active (malic acid metabolism and biological lactic acidification), yielding balanced titratable acidity and low VA; misalignment—oxygen ingress or poor SO2 or mal-selected strains—shifts balance toward VA elevation and off-odors. <cite id="a6a66f7b-0">Oxygen limits acetic acid formation under anaerobiosis; oxygen management plus SO2 reduces VA</cite>. <cite id="5ef2f7f7-0">Strain selection and co-fermentation can reduce acetic acid and keep VA in range</cite>. <cite id="10a142bb-0">Non-Saccharomyces combinations can stabilize acidity without increasing acetic acid, reduce ethanol, and lower SO2 needs</cite>.

In sum, non-Saccharomyces yeasts can either increase or decrease wine acidity depending on species, strain, oxygen exposure, fermentation stage, and co-inoculation; when oxygen and spoilage risks are controlled and beneficial deacidification/acidification strategies are applied in the right temporal window, competing mechanisms can neutralize each other, producing wines with balanced titratable acidity and acceptable volatile acidity. <cite id="5ef2f7f7-0">Non-Saccharomyces effects on acetic acid and acidity are strain- and strategy-dependent, with co-inoculation and sequential fermentations reducing acetic acid and keeping VA low</cite>. <cite id="5ef2f7f7-2">Non-Saccharomyces are now used to modulate acidity, deacidify, and improve mouthfeel while reducing ethanol</cite>. <cite id="a6a66f7b-0">Brettanomyces-driven volatile acidity is dominated by acetic acid and is oxygen-activated, mitigable by oxygen and SO2 control</cite>. <cite id="10a142bb-0">Biological MLF-like co-fermentations can replace chemical MLF, stabilize acidity without acetic acid increase, and improve sensory profile</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Ester Formation and Aroma Modulation by Non-Saccharomyces Yeasts in Wine Fermentation: A Scoping Review
Snippet: Historically, non-Saccharomyces yeasts belonging to species such as Hanseniaspora uvarum were associated with elevated acetic acid production and, consequently, with the risk of increased volatile acidity in wines. However, recent studies demonstrate that this behavior depends strongly on the strain employed and the fermentative strategy adopted [49]. Co-inoculation of the selected strain QTX-C10 with S. cerevisiae, for example, reduced final acetic acid levels by 10.81% to 17.78% [5]. Likewise, sequential fermentations involving species such as Kazachstania spp., Torulaspora delbrueckii, and Aureobasidium pullulans maintained volatile acidity below legal and sensory thresholds, while also promoting increased glycerol production and a moderate reduction in final alcohol content [46]. 

In the same context, Mylona et al. [74] reviewed the role of the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe. Formerly considered an enological spoilage agent due to the accumulation of acetic acid, hydrogen sulfide, and acetaldehyde, recent clonal selection has identified balanced strains capable of maintaining their beneficial properties without causing qualitative losses. Furthermore, although certain species exhibit the potential to increase volatile acidity, the sensory impacts do not always translate into perceptible defects. Boban et al. [66] demonstrated that Hanseniaspora pseudoguilliermondii in monoculture exhibited high acetic acid production, whereas Candida zemplinina generated the highest volatile acidity reported in the study by Beckner Whitener et al. [69] (1.37 g/L). Despite the elevated analytical value, panelists did not classify the wines as defective, but rather as more structured. 

Beyond volatile acidity, different non-Saccharomyces yeasts exhibit the capacity to modulate other metabolites relevant to the sensory and structural balance of wines [36,39,61]. In the context of biological acidification, Lachancea thermotolerans stands out for its high production of lactic acid [42,76,77].

Title: Bio-modulating wine acidity: The role of non-Saccharomyces yeasts
Snippet: In recent years, wine consumers have been looking for fruitier wines, with less ethanol, but presenting a good balance in terms of mouthfeel. However, due to the effects of global climate change, wines can be more alcoholic and flatter in terms of acidity. If in the past, non-Saccharomyces yeasts were often considered as spoilage yeasts, now they are used to modulate wine composition, namely in terms of aroma and acidity. In this article, the ability of some non-Saccharomyces yeasts to modulate wine acidity is reviewed.

Title: The Use of Yeast Mixed Cultures for Deacidification and Improvement of the Composition of Cold Climate Grape Wines
Snippet: However, due to problems associated (production of biogenic amines, ethyl carbamate, changes in the organoleptic characteristics of wine), alternative techniques are sought to reduce the acidity of wines. Deacidification using yeast strains has many benefits. It contributes to the degradation of L-malic acid but also reduces the risk of the formation of undesired compounds. Moreover, simultaneous alcoholic fermentation and deacidification prevent wine spoilage due to oxidation and inhibit the growth of harmful microorganisms. Therefore, the deacidification of wines with yeast offers the possibility of introducing better strategies to optimize the vinification process. 

A few decades ago, the term "non-Saccharomyces" was usually associated with wine spoilage, mainly due to the increase in volatile acidity or formation of undesirable compounds such as volatile phenols (for which representatives of Brettanomyces genus were responsible) [10,11]. However, over the past years, many studies have demonstrated the metabolic/enzymatic potential of certain non-Saccharomyces yeasts, and their role in improving some technological and sensory aspects of wine [12][13][14]. The application of non-Saccharomyces yeasts has become a trend in the modern wine industry. Currently, several species of non-Saccharomyces yeast are used on an industrial scale, including Torulaspora delbrueckii, Lachancea thermotolerans, Metschnikowia pulcherrima and Pichia kluyveri. The advantage of their application is, among others, modification of the aroma [15,16], control of acidity [17], improvement of color and mouthfeel properties [18], as well as decreasing the ethanol content in wines [19,20]. In recent years, the number of studies using non-Saccharomyces yeast has increased significantly. However, still many species have not yet been well investigated, including yeasts of Candida, Hanseniaspora/Kloeckera, Metschnikowia, Pichia, Torulaspora and Zygosaccharomyces genera.

Title: Advances in the Quality Improvement of Fruit Wines: A Review
Snippet: Fruit wine like blueberry wine fermented with industrial Saccharomyces yeasts usually has an excessively sour taste caused by high contents of residual organic acids, negatively affecting the flavor and quality of blueberry wine [55]. Fermentation with non-Saccharomyces yeasts could potentially solve this problem. Wang et al. found that titratable acidity was decreased in blueberry wine using pure T. delbrueckii when compared to Saccharomyces yeast inoculation [9], which could attribute to the decreased malic acid and citric acid contents [56]. A Pichia fermentans yeast also had a strong ability to degrade citric acid during blueberry wine fermentation [55]. Likewise, Hanseniaspora uvarum and M. pulcherrima reduced the titratable acidity in peach wine, mainly attributing to the reduced malic acid [10]. 

Regarding volatile compounds, increasing evidence demonstrated the positive contributions of non-Saccharomyces yeasts on the improvement of aroma complexity and sensory perception of fruit wines. Padilla et al. have concluded which non-Saccharomyces yeast species produced higher or lower volatile compounds in wine [41]. For instance, M. pulcherrima, Candida zemplinina, and Lachancea thermotolerans were described as higher producers of higher alcohols. M. pulcherrima still seems to be a strong producer of higher alcohols in peach wine [10] and bilberry wine [49], in accordance with its fermentation characteristics in wine [33]. Nevertheless, pure M. pulcherrima fermentation led to a decrease in higher alcohols in mango wine [57], indicating the impact of fruit matrices on higher alcohols during fermentation.

Historically, non-Saccharomyces yeasts belonging to species such as Hanseniaspora uvarum were associated with elevated acetic acid production and, consequently, with the risk of increased volatile acidity in wines. However, recent studies demonstrate that this behavior depends strongly on the strain employed and the fermentative strategy adopted [49]. Co-inoculation of the selected strain QTX-C10 with S. cerevisiae, for example, reduced final acetic acid levels by 10.81% to 17.78% [5]. Likewise, sequential fermentations involving species such as Kazachstania spp., Torulaspora delbrueckii, and Aureobasidium pullulans maintained volatile acidity below legal and sensory thresholds, while also promoting increased glycerol production and a moderate reduction in final alcohol content [46]. 

In the same context, Mylona et al. [74] reviewed the role of the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe. Formerly considered an enological spoilage agent due to the accumulation of acetic acid, hydrogen sulfide, and acetaldehyde, recent clonal selection has identified balanced strains capable of maintaining their beneficial properties without causing qualitative losses. Furthermore, although certain species exhibit the potential to increase volatile acidity, the sensory impacts do not always translate into perceptible defects. Boban et al. [66] demonstrated that Hanseniaspora pseudoguilliermondii in monoculture exhibited high acetic acid production, whereas Candida zemplinina generated the highest volatile acidity reported in the study by Beckner Whitener et al. snippet.text: In recent years, wine consumers have been looking for fruitier wines, with less ethanol, but presenting a good balance in terms of mouthfeel. However, due to the effects of global climate change, wines can be more alcoholic and flatter in terms of acidity. If in the past, non-Saccharomyces yeasts were often considered as spoilage yeasts, now they are used to modulate wine composition, namely in terms of aroma and acidity. In this article, the ability of some non-Saccharomyces yeasts to modulate wine acidity is reviewed.

However, due to problems associated (production of biogenic amines, ethyl carbamate, changes in the organoleptic characteristics of wine), alternative techniques are sought to reduce the acidity of wines. Deacidification using yeast strains has many benefits. It contributes to the degradation of L-malic acid but also reduces the risk of the formation of undesired compounds. Moreover, simultaneous alcoholic fermentation and deacidification prevent wine spoilage due to oxidation and inhibit the growth of harmful microorganisms. Therefore, the deacidification of wines with yeast offers the possibility of introducing better strategies to optimize the vinification process. 

A few decades ago, the term "non-Saccharomyces" was usually associated with wine spoilage, mainly due to the increase in volatile acidity or formation of undesirable compounds such as volatile phenols (for which representatives of Brettanomyces genus were responsible) [10,11]. However, over the past years, many studies have demonstrated the metabolic/enzymatic potential of certain non-Saccharomyces yeasts, and their role in improving some technological and sensory aspects of wine [12][13][14]. The application of non-Saccharomyces yeasts has become a trend in the modern wine industry. Currently, several species of non-Saccharomyces yeast are used on an industrial scale, including Torulaspora delbrueckii, Lachancea thermotolerans, Metschnikowia pulcherrima and Pichia kluyveri. The advantage of their application is, among others, modification of the aroma [15,16], control of acidity [17], improvement of color and mouthfeel properties [18], as well as decreasing the ethanol content in wines [19,20]. In recent years, the number of studies using non-Saccharomyces yeast has increased significantly. However, still many species have not yet been well investigated, including yeasts of Candida, Hanseniaspora/Kloeckera, Metschnikowia, Pichia, Torulaspora and Zygosaccharomyces genera.

Fruit wine like blueberry wine fermented with industrial Saccharomyces yeasts usually has an excessively sour taste caused by high contents of residual organic acids, negatively affecting the flavor and quality of blueberry wine [55]. Fermentation with non-Saccharomyces yeasts could potentially solve this problem. Wang et al. found that titratable acidity was decreased in blueberry wine using pure T. delbrueckii when compared to Saccharomyces yeast inoculation [9], which could attribute to the decreased malic acid and citric acid contents [56]. A Pichia fermentans yeast also had a strong ability to degrade citric acid during blueberry wine fermentation [55]. Likewise, Hanseniaspora uvarum and M. pulcherrima reduced the titratable acidity in peach wine, mainly attributing to the reduced malic acid [10]. 

Regarding volatile compounds, increasing evidence demonstrated the positive contributions of non-Saccharomyces yeasts on the improvement of aroma complexity and sensory perception of fruit wines. Padilla et al. have concluded which non-Saccharomyces yeast species produced higher or lower volatile compounds in wine [41]. For instance, M. pulcherrima, Candida zemplinina, and Lachancea thermotolerans were described as higher producers of higher alcohols. M. pulcherrima still seems to be a strong producer of higher alcohols in peach wine [10] and bilberry wine [49], in accordance with its fermentation characteristics in wine [33]. Nevertheless, pure M. pulcherrima fermentation led to a decrease in higher alcohols in mango wine [57], indicating the impact of fruit matrices on higher alcohols during fermentation.

Title: Significance of Brettanomyces and Dekkera during winemaking: a synoptic review.
Snippet: Brettanomyces/Dekkera spp. have long been known for their ability to affect wine quality negatively through the formation of acetic acid, which constitutes more than 90% of wine's volatile acidity (VA) (Van der Walt & Van Kerken, 1958). Elevated levels of acetic acid can be detrimental to wine quality as it imparts a vinegary/ acetone-like aroma (Eglinton & Henschke, 1999) and has also been associated with sluggish/stuck fermentations (Bisson, 1999). Brettanomyces/Dekkera yeasts have a particular metabolism that enables them to produce acetic acid (Licker et al. 1998;Loureiro & Malfeito-Ferreira, 2006). M.T.J. Custers was the first to describe that the presence of oxygen stimulated glucose fermentation and that this led to the introduction of a biochemical characteristic known as the "negative Pasteur effect" (or 'Custers' effect') (Scheffers & Wiken, 1969;Wijsman et al., 1984;Licker et al., 1998). Custers also determined that several strains of Brettanomyces were capable of producing considerable quantities of acetic acid under conditions of aerobiosis and found that anaerobic conditions inhibited glucose fermentation (Licker et al. 1998). 

Recently, studies have shown that the availability of oxygen presents a favourable scenario for the development of Brettanomyces/Dekkera yeasts during winemaking as it supports their growth and survival and also acetic acid production (Ciani et al., 1997;Freer et al., 2003;Aguilar-Uscanga et al., 2003). In contrast, anaerobosis during alcoholic fermentation may well impede Brettanomyces/Dekkera growth, but would not necessarily prevent their development (Ciani et al., 1997). Therefore, the risk involved with VA formation by Brettanomyces/Dekkera spp. can be reduced by minimising the wine's exposure to oxygen (during racking and transfers) in combination with effective SO 2 usage (Du Toit et al. 2005).

Title: Combine Use of Selected Schizosaccharomyces pombe and Lachancea thermotolerans Yeast Strains as an Alternative to the Traditional Malolactic Fermentation in Red Wine Production
Snippet: Most red wines commercialized in the market use the malolactic fermentation process in order to ensure stability from a microbiological point of view. In this second fermentation, malic acid is converted into l-lactic acid under controlled setups. However this process is not free from possible collateral effects that on some occasions produce off-flavors, wine quality loss and human health problems. In warm viticulture regions such as the south of Spain, the risk of suffering a deviation during the malolactic fermentation process increases due to the high must pH. This contributes to produce wines with high volatile acidity and biogenic amine values. This manuscript develops a new red winemaking methodology that consists of combining the use of two non-Saccharomyces yeast strains as an alternative to the traditional malolactic fermentation. In this method, malic acid is totally consumed by Schizosaccharomyces pombe, thus achieving the microbiological stabilization objective, while Lachancea thermotolerans produces lactic acid in order not to reduce and even increase the acidity of wines produced from low acidity musts. This technique reduces the risks inherent to the malolactic fermentation process when performed in warm regions. The result is more fruity wines that contain less acetic acid and biogenic amines than the traditional controls that have undergone the classical malolactic fermentation.

Title: The effect of micro-oxygenation on the phenolic composition, quality and aerobic wine-spoilage microorganisms of different South African red wines
Snippet: Acetic acid bacteria and Brettanomyces are both well-known spoilage microorganisms of wine. Acetic acid bacteria can form elevated levels of acetic acid through the oxidative metabolism of ethanol. Brettanomyces can cause medicinal/barnyard characteristics in wine due to the production of volatile phenols. Both the abovementioned organisms have been proven to grow in wine when oxygen levels are increased (Du Toit & Pretorius, 2002;Du Toit et al., 2005). According to our knowledge, to date, the effect of micro-oxygenation on acetic acid bacteria and Brettanomyces cell numbers in wine has not been reported. Figures 9 and 10 show the acetic acid bacteria and Brettanomyces numbers in wine C during micro-oxygenation. Acetic acid bacteria numbers decreased in the control tank after four weeks, but were generally higher in the tanks receiving O 2 and in the barrel (Fig. 9). Acetic acid bacteria can reach a viable but non-culturable state in wine that can be negated by the addition of O2, as could happen when micro-oxygenation is applied to the wine (Du Toit et al., 2005). 

Brettanomyces counts increased in the 1.5 mg 02/L/month treatment from 10 1 to 10 3 cfu/mL after 14 weeks (Fig. 10). At this point the free SO 2 concentration decreased in this tank to 18 mg/L, and was then increased to 35 mg/L. This led to a decrease in Brettanomyces cell counts in this tank. The counts in the 3 mg 02/L/month tank increased, with a correlating decrease in the free SO 2 (17 mg/L) at week 20. At this stage, the SO 2 was then adjusted to 35 mg/L in all the treatments. Therefore, micro-oxygenation does not seem to support the growth of acetic acid bacteria but possibly supports their survival. With the permeation of O2 through oak staves (Vivas et al., 2003), small amounts of O2 coming into contact with wine could hence support the survival of acetic acid bacteria and Brettanomyces in the barrel and oxygentreated wines.

This correlates with high ethanol production and ethanol tolerance. snippet.text: Most red wines commercialized in the market use the malolactic fermentation process in order to ensure stability from a microbiological point of view. In this second fermentation, malic acid is converted into l-lactic acid under controlled setups. However this process is not free from possible collateral effects that on some occasions produce off-flavors, wine quality loss and human health problems. In warm viticulture regions such as the south of Spain, the risk of suffering a deviation during the malolactic fermentation process increases due to the high must pH. This contributes to produce wines with high volatile acidity and biogenic amine values. This manuscript develops a new red winemaking methodology that consists of combining the use of two non-Saccharomyces yeast strains as an alternative to the traditional malolactic fermentation. In this method, malic acid is totally consumed by Schizosaccharomyces pombe, thus achieving the microbiological stabilization objective, while Lachancea thermotolerans produces lactic acid in order not to reduce and even increase the acidity of wines produced from low acidity musts. This technique reduces the risks inherent to the malolactic fermentation process when performed in warm regions. The result is more fruity wines that contain less acetic acid and biogenic amines than the traditional controls that have undergone the classical malolactic fermentation.

snippet.text:
Acetic acid bacteria and Brettanomyces are both well-known spoilage microorganisms of wine. Acetic acid bacteria can form elevated levels of acetic acid through the oxidative metabolism of ethanol. Brettanomyces can cause medicinal/barnyard characteristics in wine due to the production of volatile phenols. Both the abovementioned organisms have been proven to grow in wine when oxygen levels are increased (Du Toit & Pretorius, 2002;Du Toit et al., 2005). According to our knowledge, to date, the effect of micro-oxygenation on acetic acid bacteria and Brettanomyces cell numbers in wine has not been reported. Figures 9 and 10 show the acetic acid bacteria and Brettanomyces numbers in wine C during micro-oxygenation. Acetic acid bacteria numbers decreased in the control tank after four weeks, but were generally higher in the tanks receiving O 2 and in the barrel (Fig. 9). Acetic acid bacteria can reach a viable but non-culturable state in wine that can be negated by the addition of O2, as could happen when micro-oxygenation is applied to the wine (Du Toit et al., 2005). 

Brettanomyces counts increased in the 1.5 mg 02/L/month treatment from 10 1 to 10 3 cfu/mL after 14 weeks (Fig. 10). At this point the free SO 2 concentration decreased in this tank to 18 mg/L, and was then increased to 35 mg/L. This led to a decrease in Brettanomyces cell counts in this tank. The counts in the 3 mg 02/L/month tank increased, with a correlating decrease in the free SO 2 (17 mg/L) at week 20. At this stage, the SO 2 was then adjusted to 35 mg/L in all the treatments. Therefore, micro-oxygenation does not seem to support the growth of acetic acid bacteria but possibly supports their survival. With the permeation of O2 through oak staves (Vivas et al., 2003), small amounts of O2 coming into contact with wine could hence support the survival of acetic acid bacteria and Brettanomyces in the barrel and oxygentreated wines.

documents.title: Significance of Brettanomyces and Dekkera during winemaking: a synoptic review.
documents.snippet:
Brettanomyces/Dekkera spp. have long been known for their ability to affect wine quality negatively through the formation of acetic acid, which constitutes more than 90% of wine's volatile acidity (VA) (Van der Walt & Van Kerken, 1958). Elevated levels of acetic acid can be detrimental to wine quality as it imparts a vinegary/ acetone-like aroma (Eglinton & Henschke, 1999) and has also been associated with sluggish/stuck fermentations (Bisson, 1999). Brettanomyces/Dekkera yeasts have a particular metabolism that enables them to produce acetic acid (Licker et al. 1998;Loureiro & Malfeito-Ferreira, 2006). M.T.J. Custers was the first to describe that the presence of oxygen stimulated glucose fermentation and that this led to the introduction of a biochemical characteristic known as the "negative Pasteur effect" (or 'Custers' effect') (Scheffers & Wiken, 1969;Wijsman et al., 1984;Licker et al., 1998). Custers also determined that several strains of Brettanomyces were capable of producing considerable quantities of acetic acid under conditions of aerobiosis and found that anaerobic conditions inhibited glucose fermentation (Licker et al. 1998). 

Recently, studies have shown that the availability of oxygen presents a favourable scenario for the development of Brettanomyces/Dekkera yeasts during winemaking as it supports their growth and survival and also acetic acid production (Ciani et al., 1997;Freer et al., 2003;Aguilar-Uscanga et al., 2003). In contrast, anaerobosis during alcoholic fermentation may well impede Brettanomyces/Dekkera growth, but would not necessarily prevent their development (Ciani et al., 1997). Therefore, the risk involved with VA formation by Brettanomyces/Dekkera spp. can be reduced by minimising the wine's exposure to oxygen (during racking and transfers) in combination with effective SO 2 usage (Du Toit et al. 2005).

Snippet: The comparison of the results from the fermentation trials showed differences in several analyzed parameters. judgment.criterion_reasoning: The verification criterion requires identifying at least one specific non-Saccharomyces species and explaining TWO mechanistically opposing effects on acidity FROM THAT SAME SPECIES, plus specific conditions under which these effects counterbalance. The answer extensively discusses opposing mechanisms across different species (Brettanomyces for VA increase via oxygen, vs. L. thermotolerans/S. pombe for TA decrease via acid metabolism), but does NOT demonstrate that a SINGLE species has both acidity-increasing and acidity-decreasing pathways that compete within itself. For example: (1) Brettanomyces is discussed only for increasing VA through acetic acid production (oxygen-stimulated) vs. being suppressed by anaerobiosis—this is external control of one pathway, not internal opposing mechanisms. (2) L. thermotolerans is described as producing lactic acid (increasing acidity in low-acid musts) but no opposing pathway that decreases acidity is documented for this same species. (3) S. pombe consumes malic acid (decreasing TA) but no competing pathway that increases acidity is shown. The answer treats 'competing mechanisms' as inter-species dynamics or external conditions (oxygen vs. anaerobiosis) rather than intra-species mechanistic opposition. The 'neutralization' discussion focuses on when different species or environmental controls balance each other, not when one species' own pathways counteract. This fails the core requirement.

However, it fundamentally misinterprets the criterion: it discusses opposing effects from DIFFERENT species or from EXTERNAL conditions modulating a single pathway, rather than demonstrating that ONE species possesses TWO intrinsic competing mechanisms (one increasing, one decreasing acidity) that neutralize under specific conditions. This is a structural failure to meet the core requirement despite strong topical coverage.
